title: UK doctors develop non-invasive test for womb cancer in women bleeding after menopause
content:
Doctors have developed a simple test that could help rule out womb cancer in women who experience bleeding after menopause.
The approach has the potential to transform care for thousands of women each year and spare them from invasive and uncomfortable tests that can also be costly for healthcare systems.
Every year, hundreds of thousands of women worldwide are diagnosed with womb cancer. Bleeding after menopause triggers an urgent cancer referral but only about 5% to 10% of women who report bleeding have an underlying cancer.
Currently, the tests for womb cancer – an internal ultrasound scan, a biopsy of the womb lining and hysteroscopy, in which a camera is passed into the womb – are all invasive and costly.
The new test, developed at the University of Manchester and Manchester University NHS foundation trust, looks at cells collected from the urine and vaginal fluid. It is cheap and non-invasive.
In a study assessing the test, 1,864 women attending seven hospitals in north-west England with postmenopausal bleeding gave a urine sample and a vaginal fluid sample before their routine tests.
Of these women, 5% (99 of the 1,864) were diagnosed with womb cancer via a biopsy or surgery. Using the new test, cytologists unaware of the women’s diagnoses identified 80 of the 99 womb cancers and correctly returned a negative result for 93% of women who did not have womb cancer.
The findings were published in the journal Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women’s Health.
Researchers said the test was not accurate enough to rule cancer out on its own but could fast-track women at the highest risk for urgent investigation while sparing lower-risk women immediate invasive testing, with repeat sampling or full assessment if symptoms continued.
They cautioned that the samples in the study were assessed by highly trained specialist cytologists, so it was not known whether the same accuracy could be reproduced in other settings, and that the test had not been studied in women without symptoms.
Researchers said the test could be used to triage women suspected of having womb cancer, to “support rapid diagnosis, provide quick reassurance and reduce the burden of invasive testing for women with postmenopausal bleeding”.
Prof Emma Davidson, of the University of Manchester and Manchester University NHS foundation trust, said: “Bleeding after the menopause is understandably alarming for women because it can be a sign of cancer, but the vast majority of those investigated will not have the disease.
“At the moment, many women face invasive, uncomfortable tests that can be stressful as well as costly for health services before cancer can be ruled out. Our study shows that a simple test using urine and vaginal samples could help identify the women most likely to have cancer while safely reassuring many others much earlier in the diagnostic pathway.
“If further studies confirm these findings in routine practice, this approach has the potential to transform care for thousands of women every year.”

title: Le roi Philippe et la reine Mathilde de retour en province de Liège : un programme entre solidarité et patrimoine
content:
Le roi Philippe et la reine Mathilde de retour en province de Liège : un programme entre solidarité et patrimoine
Le roi Philippe et la reine Mathilde seront à Liège et Seraing le 29 septembre pour une journée consacrée notamment au handicap, à la santé mentale, à la reconversion industrielle et au patrimoine verrier.
- Publié le 23-09-2026 à 18h30
Le Roi et la Reine seront de retour en province de Liège le 29 septembre. Leur visite débutera à Liège avant de se poursuivre à Seraing, avec plusieurs étapes consacrées à des enjeux sociaux et au patrimoine industriel de la région.
Première étape au Bercail à Liège
Le couple royal commencera sa journée à l'ASBL Le Bercail, à Liège. Ce centre accueille, en résidentiel comme en ambulatoire, des adultes présentant une déficience intellectuelle.
Le Roi et la Reine y découvriront notamment "La Cabane du souvenir", un espace de recueillement permettant aux résidents de garder la mémoire des personnes décédées, qu'il s'agisse d'autres résidents ou de proches.
Les Souverains visiteront également un appartement adapté aux personnes à mobilité réduite. Ils participeront ensuite à un atelier artistique avec plusieurs résidents, au cours duquel ils contribueront à la réalisation d'une œuvre collective avec plusieurs résidents.
Le programme se poursuivra sur la place Saint-Lambert, à l'Espace Tivoli. Le Roi et la Reine y rencontreront la population liégeoise.
Du centre de Liège au Val Saint-Lambert
Les Souverains prendront ensuite la direction de Seraing et du Val Saint-Lambert. Un déjeuner thématique sera consacré à deux enjeux particulièrement présents dans la région : la reconversion industrielle ainsi que la santé mentale et les addictions.
La visite se poursuivra dans la célèbre cristallerie sérésienne, qui fête cette année ses 200 ans. Fondée en 1826 sur le site d'une ancienne abbaye, la Cristallerie du Val Saint-Lambert perpétue depuis deux siècles un savoir-faire verrier emblématique du "Made in Belgium".
Après une présentation consacrée à l'histoire de la cristallerie et à la reconversion du site, le Roi et la Reine découvriront le musée et plusieurs pièces emblématiques, dont le célèbre "Vase des Neuf Provinces".
La journée se terminera par une démonstration de soufflage du verre dans les ateliers de la cristallerie.
Cette visite sera la première venue commune du roi Philippe et de la reine Mathilde en province de Liège depuis octobre 2023.

title: [Research] Applications and challenges of artificial intelligence in cancer management
content:
Abstract
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming cancer management by enabling the analysis of complex multimodal data generated across the cancer care continuum. This structured narrative review synthesizes current applications of AI, machine learning, and deep learning in cancer detection, imaging diagnosis, tumor characterization, histopathology, genomics, drug discovery, precision oncology, prognosis, treatment-response prediction, clinical decision support, adherence monitoring, and supportive care. A literature search was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar for publications from July 2001 to November 2025. From 564 identified records, 234 articles were included in the final thematic synthesis after duplicate removal, title/abstract screening, and full-text assessment. The reviewed evidence shows that AI models, including convolutional neural networks, U-Net-based segmentation models, radiomics approaches, hybrid models, multiple-instance learning, federated learning, large language models, and multimodal frameworks, have demonstrated substantial potential in extracting clinically meaningful patterns from imaging, pathology, genomic, biomarker, and clinical data. These tools may support earlier detection, improved tumor classification, non-invasive molecular profiling, treatment optimization, and personalized decision-making. However, clinical readiness remains uneven, as many models are limited by retrospective designs, dataset heterogeneity, data leakage, overfitting, limited explainability, insufficient external validation, and uncertain generalizability across global healthcare settings. Future progress will require diverse multicenter datasets, standardized annotation, transparent reporting, explainable and hybrid modelling, ethical data governance, regulatory oversight, and post-deployment monitoring. AI should therefore be viewed as clinician-supervised decision support that can strengthen precision oncology when implemented responsibly.
Similar content being viewed by others
1 Introduction
Cancer, the second leading cause of death globally, represents a major public health burden, defined by uncontrolled cell division and aberrant proliferation with capacity for rapid dissemination throughout the body [1]. One of the major challenges in cancer management is the highly heterogeneous and dynamic nature of the tumors, which can vary substantially across patients, cancer subtypes, and even within the same tumor over time. In addition, clinicians must interpret large volumes of multi-modal data, including radiological imaging, histopathology, genomic sequencing, and longitudinal clinical records to support accurate diagnosis, prognostic assessment, treatment selection, and disease monitoring. Conventional analytical approaches often struggle to integrate these complex and continuously evolving datasets efficiently, creating a need for intelligent computational systems capable of extracting clinically meaningful patterns from diverse data sources [2]. In recent years, the management of cancer is undergoing a transformative shift driven by advances in precision medicine, artificial intelligence (AI), and next-generation technologies. Precision oncology allows the clinicians to tailor therapies based on individual biomarkers, improving efficacy and minimizing toxicity. Simultaneously, AI is redefining the diagnostic and prognostic capabilities by facilitating the analysis of large, complex multi-modal data, from genomics and pathology to imaging and clinical records. It is being integrated at all stages of a patient’s cancer journey, cancer diagnosis, care decision support, etc. Innovative technologies such as liquid biopsies, digital pathology, next-generation sequencing, and AI-guided radiology offer real-time insights into tumour growth and treatment response, allowing for dynamic and adaptive management strategies. Furthermore, integrative platforms that combine clinical data with machine learning models seem to be useful for early detection, risk minimization, and personalized care pathways. As these integrative platforms and technologies continue to develop using AI, they are poised to not only improve outcomes but also fundamentally reshape and revolutionize how cancer is diagnosed, monitored and treated – marking a change in the field of oncology [3,4,5,6].
AI is increasingly being investigated as a tool to address these challenges. Broadly, AI refers to computational systems that can learn patterns from representative data and apply those patterns to support prediction, classification, or decision-making in new cases [7]. Machine learning (ML), a major branch of AI, enables algorithms to identify relationships within structured or semi-structured datasets, while deep learning (DL) uses multilayer neural networks to process complex data such as images, genomic profiles, and clinical records [8, 9]. Depending on the clinical problem and data type, ML approaches may involve supervised, semi-supervised, unsupervised, or reinforcement learning strategies [10].
Recent advances in AI have further expanded its relevance beyond image recognition and conventional prediction tasks. In molecular biology and drug discovery, AlphaFold has demonstrated the ability of AI to predict protein structures with near-experimental accuracy, creating new opportunities for target identification, structure-based drug design, and understanding disease-associated molecular mechanisms. The broader impact of AlphaFold on molecular biology and drug discovery has also been highlighted through recent machine-learning-driven bibliometric and informatics analyses, which show its rapidly growing influence across biomedical research [11, 12]. In parallel, large language models (LLMs) are emerging as important tools in medicine because of their capacity to process, summarize, and generate clinically relevant text, including medical literature, patient records, reports, and decision-support information. Recent reviews and bibliometric analyses have described the growing role of LLMs in medical research, diagnostic reasoning, clinical documentation, and patient-facing communication, while also emphasizing concerns regarding accuracy, bias, privacy, transparency, and clinical accountability [13, 14]. These developments provide important context for oncology, where AI systems increasingly need to integrate molecular, imaging, pathological, and clinical information to support early detection, tumor characterization, therapeutic decision-making, drug discovery, and longitudinal monitoring.
Different AI architectures are suited to different challenges in cancer care. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are particularly effective for recognizing spatial patterns in radiological, dermoscopic, and histopathological images, making them useful for tumor detection, classification, and image-based diagnosis. U-Net and related encoder–decoder architectures are widely used for segmentation tasks because they can delineate tumor boundaries and anatomical structures, which is essential for radiotherapy planning, surgical guidance, lesion-volume assessment, and disease monitoring. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), transformer-based models, and other sequential learning approaches can process temporal or text-based information, including radiology reports, pathology reports, electronic health records, and longitudinal patient data, thereby supporting automated reporting, risk prediction, and dynamic monitoring [15,16,17,18,19,20]. Hybrid and multimodal AI models further extend these capabilities by integrating imaging, pathology, genomic, biomarker, and clinical data to support precision oncology.
The overall scope of AI integration in cancer management is summarized in Fig. 1, which illustrates how multimodal data sources can be processed through AI-based methods to support different stages of cancer care. As shown in the figure, AI applications extend beyond diagnosis alone and include early detection, tumor characterization, prognostic modelling, treatment-response prediction, longitudinal monitoring, and clinical decision support. This review therefore synthesizes current applications of AI, ML, and DL in cancer management, with emphasis on detection, diagnosis, imaging, histopathology, genomics, drug discovery, prognosis, treatment optimization, monitoring, and responsible clinical implementation. The review also critically discusses major translational challenges, including dataset heterogeneity, model generalizability, overfitting, data leakage, reproducibility, explainability, ethical governance, and regulatory readiness.
2 Methods
This review was designed as a structured narrative review rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis. The objective was to provide a broad thematic synthesis of AI applications across the cancer care continuum, including diagnosis, imaging, pathology, genomics, drug discovery, treatment-response prediction, clinical decision support, monitoring, and implementation challenges. Because the scope was intentionally broad and heterogeneous, the review did not aim to answer a narrowly defined research question, perform quantitative pooling, or conduct formal risk-of-bias grading across included studies. Instead, structured search and screening procedures were used to improve transparency, reproducibility, and coverage of the literature.
An extensive literature search was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar, covering publications from July 2001 to November 2025. Search terms included “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” “deep learning,” “cancer detection,” “tumor characterization,” “precision oncology,” “drug discovery,” “next-generation sequencing,” and “clinical decision support.” Boolean operators including “AND” and “OR” were applied to refine the search, and filters for English-language peer-reviewed articles were used where available. Reference lists of key articles were also screened manually to identify additional relevant studies.
The selection process followed a stepwise workflow. Retrieved records were first screened for duplication. Titles and abstracts were then reviewed to exclude clearly irrelevant articles. Study selection was conducted by two independent reviewers. In the first stage, titles and abstracts were screened for relevance based on the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. In the second stage, potentially eligible articles were assessed through full-text review. Disagreements at either stage were resolved through discussion and consensus; when consensus could not be reached, a third reviewer was consulted. This process was used to minimize selection bias and improve consistency in article inclusion. Potentially eligible articles underwent full-text assessment and were retained if they contributed directly to one or more predefined thematic domains, including cancer detection, diagnosis, imaging, histopathology, genomics, drug discovery, prognostic modelling, treatment optimization, monitoring, and clinical decision support. Articles were excluded if they were not cancer-focused, did not involve AI/ML/DL approaches, lacked full-text availability, were not peer-reviewed, or did not provide sufficient methodological or conceptual relevance to the scope of the review. The literature search initially identified 564 records, of which 234 were included in the final narrative synthesis after duplicate removal, title/abstract screening, and full-text assessment. The reporting of the search and selection process was therefore informed by PRISMA principles where appropriate, particularly in documenting database sources, search terms, screening stages, and the flow of article selection. However, the manuscript should not be interpreted as a full PRISMA-based systematic review because the final synthesis was narrative and thematic rather than quantitative. A PRISMA-like flow diagram (Fig. 2) was included to transparently show how the initial 564 records were reduced to the 234 articles included in the final synthesis.
Because this was a structured narrative review and not a systematic review of intervention effects, formal risk-of-bias scoring was not undertaken. Nevertheless, included studies were assessed for methodological and thematic relevance based on peer-reviewed status, relevance to AI/ML/DL in oncology, clarity of study objectives, adequacy of dataset or model description, reporting of performance metrics where applicable, and contribution to the thematic synthesis. The reporting of the review was guided by principles consistent with SANRA, particularly clarity of review aims, transparency of literature search, appropriate referencing, and balanced presentation of evidence.
3 Applications of AI in cancer management
3.1 Cancer imaging
There is an increasing demand for noninvasive imaging to monitor treatment response and yield clinically relevant tumor information as part of the strategy for contemporary cancer treatment. Figure 3 illustrates the use of AI in detecting and classifying tumors in various anatomical regions and Table 1 lists some of the diverse applications of AI in cancer imaging based on the cancer site, for early detection, characterization, and tumor monitoring [21].
Although many AI-based imaging models have demonstrated encouraging diagnostic performance, these findings should be interpreted cautiously because reported outcomes are not directly comparable across studies. Performance estimates vary according to cancer type, imaging modality, dataset size, annotation quality, scanner protocol, patient demographics, and validation strategy. In particular, models trained and tested on single-institution or retrospectively curated datasets may not retain the same accuracy when applied to external populations or real-world clinical workflows. Therefore, the current evidence should be understood as a spectrum ranging from proof-of-concept models to externally validated and prospectively evaluated clinical tools.
3.1.1 Early tumor detection
The use of conventional computer-aided diagnosis (CADx) in cancer detection by radiologists has significantly improved identification, interpretation time and accurate detection of abnormalities. However, the CADx system does not detect nodules and does not have a good level of automation. As a result, recent computer-assisted technologies for cancer diagnosis have incorporated deep-learning AI systems that have shown improved performance over conventional CADx systems in selected diagnostic tasks. However, such improvements are task- and dataset-dependent, and superiority should not be assumed across all cancer types, imaging modalities, or clinical settings without external validation [22].
Blood-based tests and liquid biopsies hold potential for early detection of cancer but are limited by the low detection sensitivity of certain biomarkers. For instance, biomarkers such as circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) levels can increase to 10% or greater in advanced stages of cancer, thus enabling cancer detection and disease monitoring compared to early-stage cancer in which case, the median concentration of ctDNA is much lower, (notably at least 1000 times lower), thus making early cancer detection difficult [23]. Therefore, the need to develop healthcare instruments capable of detecting such biomarkers and mutations in blood at very low concentrations for early detection of cancer is essential. AI can substantially enhance blood-based cancer detection by rapidly analyzing large number of proteomic signatures associated with cancer-related proteins and nucleic acid molecules, including exosomes and microRNAs [24]. Moreover, AI can identify biomarkers and/or patterns that signal the presence of malignant tumors (cancer) much earlier compared to the current methods, thus assisting in early cancer detection [25].
DL-based AI models like deep neural networks (DNN) have been reported through multiple studies for accurate cancer diagnosis and subtype identification directly from histopathological images, such as H&E-stained whole slide images of tissue derived from biopsies or surgical resections [26, 27]. It also has the ability to infer genetic mutations directly from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histopathology slides [28, 29], and multiple “pan-cancer” studies have validated the feasibility of deep learning-based prediction of biomarkers across all human cancers [30,31,32]. Furthermore, in a study by Nam et al., a DL-based AI model enhanced the performance of physicians in detecting malignant lung nodules, together, corroborating the increased probability of a more accurate detection of cancer using AI based models [33]. However, many such models remain at the proof-of-concept or retrospective validation stage, and their clinical utility depends on reproducible performance across external datasets, standardized slide preparation, scanner variability, annotation quality, and prospective clinical evaluation. A comprehensive list of applications of AI in cancer detection and diagnosis is shown in Table 1.
3.1.2 Tumor characterization
Characterization of a tumor includes its segmentation, diagnosis, and staging. Currently, tumors are manually defined, which is time-consuming and limits experts through inconsistent reproducibility [54, 55]. With advances in computing speed and AI algorithm efficiency, automated segmentation can now improve the quality, reproducibility, and consistency of tumor measurements.
Diagnosis of suspicious lesions as benign or malignant is carried out by radiologists through the visual interpretation of radiologic data, and staging includes classifying tumors into specific groups depending on their appearance and spread, which correlates with the expected clinical course of the cancer as well as the treatment strategies [21]. Despite human experience and expertise being of high value, inconsistent interpretation among human readers has been reported [56, 57]. CADx system that performs a diagnosis of lesions to make a distinction between benign and malignant tumors is a useful tool for radiologists to accurately diagnose malignant lesions [58,59,60]. Studies have demonstrated that CADx systems can stage tumors by evaluating tumor extent and multifocality on breast magnetic resonance imaging, as well as through automated lesion volume measurement in breast magnetic resonance mammography [61, 62]. However, there are certain limitations of CADx as well, which could be overcome with the use of AI. AI algorithms can substantially enhance the sensitivity and specificity of liquid biopsy, reinforcing its reliability as a cancer screening tool. By improving discrimination between benign and malignant tumors, AI reduces false positives and unnecessary interventions, ultimately refining tumor diagnosis and staging, facilitating earlier and more targeted treatment, and improving patient survival outcomes [25].
The use of AI in the characterization of cancer is summarized in Table 2.
Taken together, Tables 1 and 2 indicate that AI applications in cancer detection and characterization are concentrated around four broad methodological categories: conventional machine-learning models, deep-learning models, radiomics-based approaches, and hybrid or multimodal models. This pattern is consistent with major reviews of AI in cancer imaging, which describe applications across detection, diagnosis, tumor segmentation, radiomics, treatment-response prediction, and prognostic modelling [21, 83]. Conventional machine-learning methods, such as support vector machines, random forests, k-nearest neighbors, and logistic regression, are commonly applied to handcrafted imaging, radiomics, or structured clinical features. These models can be relatively interpretable and suitable for smaller datasets, but their performance depends heavily on feature selection, preprocessing, segmentation quality, and dataset composition. Radiomics-based approaches similarly provide quantitative tumor phenotyping through handcrafted shape, intensity, and texture features, supporting tumor characterization, prognosis, and treatment-response prediction [83].
Deep-learning models, particularly CNN-based architectures, 3D-CNNs, and U-Net-based segmentation models, are widely used across CT, MRI, ultrasound, mammography, PET/CT, dermoscopy, and histopathology because they can learn complex spatial patterns directly from images. However, they generally require large, diverse, and well-annotated datasets and remain vulnerable to overfitting, poor external generalization, and limited interpretability. Large reviews of diagnostic deep-learning studies have also noted that although performance can be promising, external validation, transparent reporting, and fair comparison with clinicians are often limited [84, 85]. Hybrid and multimodal models attempt to combine the strengths of these approaches by integrating handcrafted features, deep-learning-derived features, imaging data, clinical variables, and molecular or genomic information. These approaches are especially relevant to precision oncology because imaging-based AI may support prognosis, treatment-response prediction, molecular-profile inference, and clinical decision support when combined with complementary biological and clinical data [83].
Across the reviewed studies, CT and MRI were the most frequently represented modalities, particularly for lung, pancreatic, liver, brain, breast, and head-and-neck cancers, whereas ultrasound, mammography, dermoscopy, PET/CT, and histopathology provided site-specific diagnostic or prognostic value. Overall, the evidence suggests that AI is most mature for image-based detection, classification, and segmentation tasks, while applications involving survival prediction, molecular characterization, treatment-response prediction, and clinical decision support still require stronger external validation, prospective testing, and standardized reporting before routine clinical adoption [21, 85]. 3.1.3 Tumour monitoring
Conventional approaches for monitoring tumor response, such as the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) and WHO criteria, rely on predefined measurements to estimate treatment response or tumor burden [86]. While widely used and found to improve survival, these metrics have significant limitations, including oversimplification of tumor geometry and the inability to account for therapeutic changes in certain lesion types such as osseous (bone) lesions, which may not shrink in size despite a positive response to chemotherapy and improved patient survival [87]. In this context, AI-driven monitoring offers a promising alternative, as it can analyze a significantly vast number of complex imaging features over time, many of which may be overlooked by human. AI-based tools can also enable automated registration of serial images, precise segmentation of tumors, and data-driven diagnostics.
3.2 Drug discovery and precision medicine
Traditional cancer treatments such as chemotherapy and radiation often have limited specificity and may cause systemic toxicity, which has contributed to the development of precision oncology as a more individualized therapeutic approach [88]. Precision oncology aims to tailor treatment strategies according to the molecular characteristics of an individual patient’s tumor, enabling more effective and potentially less toxic cancer therapy compared with the traditional one-size-fits-all approach [89]. In this context, AI models can support precision oncology by predicting compound–target interactions, identifying suitable patient cohorts, optimizing trial design, and forecasting clinical trial outcomes [90]. The integration of high-throughput technologies, including proteomics, next-generation sequencing (NGS), metabolomics, and other omics platforms, has accelerated the identification of biomarkers and molecular targets associated with specific cancer subtypes [91]. This progress has supported the development of targeted therapies, including trastuzumab for HER2-positive breast cancer and vemurafenib for BRAF-mutant melanoma [92]. Similarly, vemurafenib demonstrated improved survival outcomes in patients with BRAF V600E-mutant melanoma, highlighting the clinical value of biomarker-guided targeted therapy [93]. Moreover, NGS and liquid biopsy technologies have improved molecular profiling, early detection, real-time monitoring of treatment response, and identification of resistance mechanisms [94]. AI has further strengthened this field by enabling the integration and interpretation of complex multi-omics data, thereby accelerating target validation and supporting the optimization of personalized therapeutic strategies [95].
3.2.1 Next-generation sequencing
NGS has revolutionized the detection of cancer-associated aberrations and mutations within the genome, offering immense potential for the advancement of precision oncology. DNA or RNA samples taken from blood, tumor tissue, cell lines, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) blocks, and liquid biopsies can be sequenced using NGS technologies [96]. RNA sequencing (RNAseq) is extensively employed in cancer research and diagnostics to analyze gene expression, investigate alterations in the cellular transcriptome and molecular pathways, and detect mutations linked to alternative splicing events [97]. A study utilizing RNAseq profiling on samples from children and young adults was conducted by Vaske and his colleagues and comparing them with tumor profiles from pediatric and young adult cancer patients available in public databases. The study was found to reveal the significant impact of precision oncology, particularly in addressing hard-to-treat pediatric cancers [98].
3.2.2 Discovery of novel targets
Discovering novel genes and molecular pathways underlying multidrug resistance is critical in cancer management, as they represent promising candidates for drug design and discovery [99]. In a recent glioblastoma study, laser capture micro-dissected RNAseq (LCM-RNAseq), a high-resolution NGS approach, revealed upregulation of growth factor signaling pathways in pseudopalisading cells relative to the tumor. The upregulated genes identified were associated with disease progression, positioning them as potential therapeutic targets in glioblastoma [100].
One of the causes of drug resistance could be epigenetic modifications, as in the case of estrogen receptor (ER) positive breast and ovarian cancer. RNAseq data from multiple studies have revealed that the mutations present in the ligand-binding domain of ER, the mutated estrogen receptor alpha gene (ESR1) present in circulating tumor DNA, and activation of the PI3K/mTOR pathways are associated with therapy resistance [101, 102]. These mutations can be therapeutic targets for future novel drugs and essential biomarkers for predicting prognosis and managing treatment options for ER-positive breast cancers.
3.3 Prognosis and treatment response prediction
Previously, clinicians ranging from specialty doctors to paramedics, were responsible for cancer prognosis and predictions. With AI technology, clinicians now have a decision support tool to better predict disease prognosis and treatment outcome [103]. It uses genetic, clinical, and lifestyle data together to recommend individualized therapies.
Considerable research has investigated semantic and automatic radiomic features for predicting treatment outcomes in cancer patients, as demonstrated by the CANARY tool (Computer Aided Nodule Assessment and Risk Yield) in identifying a high-risk subset of lung adenocarcinoma cases [64]. Emerging evidence indicates that AI can automatically quantify radiographic features of tumor phenotype, with such data holding notable prognostic value across multiple cancer types, including lung cancer and distant metastasis in lung adenocarcinoma [66, 69].
AI has also shown promise in predicting disease development according to a research group at Mount Sinai, showing an outcome of 93% accuracy in predicting the development of a variety of diseases, including prostate, rectal, and liver cancer [104]. AI is also being used to predict radiotherapy toxicity, including liver radiotherapy, resulting in hepatobiliary toxicity and cervical cancer radiotherapy leading to rectal toxicity [105, 106]. Table 2 lists some of the diverse applications of AI in clinical outcome prediction.
Moreover, AI is well-positioned to address the limitations of current targeted and immunotherapies, whose distinct clinical benefits are often inadequately captured by RECIST-based endpoints [107]. AI has recently shown promise in evaluating immunotherapy response through the identification of radiomic biomarkers. A recent study demonstrated the feasibility of a novel radiomic biomarker for predicting progression-free survival (PFS) in patients with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) receiving pembrolizumab-based therapy, revealing that image resampling mitigated heterogeneity while enhancing the prognostic value of tumor phenotypes and PFS prediction [108]. A further study reported enhanced survival prognostication by integrating genomic and radiomic data into a clinical model, confirming the complementary nature of these biomarkers and highlighting the potential of AI in uncovering predictive associations within combined datasets [65]. The assessment of treatment response to targeted therapy could thus be improved using AI analysis of quantitative imaging data (Box 1).
3.4 Clinical decision making
Al has further proven its potential for clinical data synthesis in the field of oncology, in addition to being a guide to decision making. Currently, applications are being developed using AI to match patient data with national clinical trial databases and to find appropriate investigational drugs that are currently being developed for a given patient [111]. AI can also be used in decision making by physicians in making intervention choices while dealing with patients with uncommon profiles [112]. However, such support provided by AI-based analyses is raising ethical concerns that will need to be diligently addressed, such as to whom does the responsibility lie in the event of a negative outcome caused by the information used by the AI system [113].
AI can be linked to patient data and national treatment guidelines to guide effective disease management. One such example is IBM’s Watson for Oncology (WFO) support system. WFO helps in clinical decision-making by using algorithms for treatment recommendations and has been successful in determining treatment regimens for breast cancer, gastric cancer, and non-small-cell lung cancer [114,115,116]. These studies have also shown harmony between the WFO recommendations and the medical team, and have also been reported to be quick, accurate, and effective in treatment decision making [116], demonstrating potential use for AI in low resource settings.
3.5 Cancer research
Equally important, AI has a significant impact on various aspects of cancer research and offers powerful tools to enhance the understanding, diagnosis, and treatment of cancer. As cancer encompasses a vast array of diseases characterized by uncontrolled cell proliferation and metastasis, the ability of AI to analyze complex datasets, identify subtle patterns, and generate predictive insights offers unprecedented opportunities. Machine learning tools, particularly supervised deep learning, have shown promise in analyzing MRI and ultrasound scans to spot suspicious areas and distinguish aggressive cancers from less harmful ones. Application of AI in eight common types of cancer are summarized below.
3.5.1 Blood cancer
Blood cancer, commonly known as hematological malignancy, is often the second leading cause of death from cancer. It originates from bone marrow or from cells that have the ability to form blood, and is found to be caused by genetic and environmental factors. It typically results from the abnormal growth of white blood cells, resulting in a disproportion among the blood elements [117]. As the rate of death is high, early detection is essential to ensure successful treatment. There are mainly two types of blood cancer, leukemia which also has several subtypes, and lymphoma.
Due to the complexity in the detection of early symptoms of hematological malignancies, latest AI applications in the management have gained considerable focus. Advanced deep learning techniques such as VGG19, RegNetX016, ResNetRS50, AlexNet, EfficientNet, Convnext, Xception, and Inception_V3 are being used for the detection of somatic driver mutations that characterizes the blood disease and influences therapeutic decision-making [118].
NGS is successfully being used for the diagnosis and accurate classification of hematologic malignancies based on genetic alterations. For acute myeloid leukemia, the revised WHO classification and European LeukemiaNet recommendations consider genetic abnormalities as a foremost priority for the diagnosis, treatment choice and the post-treatment monitoring of the disease [119]. Thus, the success rate of timely diagnosis and treatment options are increasing.
3.5.2 Brain cancer
Brain cancer or central nervous system (CNS) tumors are heterogeneous and impose a considerable burden on global health, with over 250,000 cases reported annually worldwide. Among these, glioblastoma stands out as a rapidly growing, aggressive malignancy and remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in affected patients [120]. The three main challenges associated with the evaluation of CNS tumors include accurate diagnosis and extent of disease prediction for making clinical decisions, tracking of the disease and spread over time and monitoring to check associated effects on surrounding tissue post treatment, and the ability to extract genotype signatures from the phenotype manifestation of tumors on imaging [21].
AI has substantially advanced diagnostic imaging in glioma by enabling tumor classification that surpasses the interpretive limits of human experts. It has been widely used to differentiate low- from high-grade tumors and individual WHO grades through machine learning classifiers trained on multimodal MRI data [74]. Deep CNNs trained on conventional MR images have further been applied to identify clinically relevant molecular subtypes, including isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status [70].
Recent advances in AI and deep learning, coupled with large-scale datasets, have generated growing interest in automated tools for detecting and monitoring metastatic cancer longitudinally. Link et al. (2024) developed longitudinal deep neural networks for assessing metastatic brain cancer on a large open benchmark, achieving state-of-the-art performance in detecting and segmenting small metastases (< 10 mm³) with strong predictive value for overall survival [121]. A recent study further developed an AI tool capable of rapid, accurate, and cost-effective brain tumor classification based on genome-wide DNA methylation profiles, with implications for biomarker discovery, compact point-of-care assay development, and future epigenomic research in brain tumors [122]. AI has been effectively utilized in predicting prognosis and treatment response with the use of multiparametric MRI combined with machine learning for pediatric low-grade glioma in a recent study as well [77]. The key challenge in brain tumor diagnosis is distinguishing primary CNS lymphoma from glioblastoma, given their frequently overlapping imaging phenotypes. While radiomics models leveraging image-based texture features have been developed to address this, there remains a pressing need for more robust predictive models capable of reliably differentiating between the two [123].
3.5.3 Breast cancer
Breast cancer is the most common cancer diagnosed in women, with an estimated prevalence of 2.3 million cases diagnosed globally each year [124, 125]. Advances in imaging technology, paired with improvements in computer-based tools, have made artificial intelligence (AI) a key part of breast cancer care. This includes estimating a patient’s risk of developing cancer, early tumor detection, and more accurate diagnosis, prognosis, and predicting response to therapy [21].
Computer-assisted tools (CADe/CADx) for detecting and diagnosing breast cancer have been in development for years [126]. The goal of CADe systems is to highlight suspicious areas; however, radiologists still make the final decisions. While CADe tools continue to advance for standard mammography, research attention has shifted toward 3D imaging modalities including ultrasound, MRI, and tomosynthesis through the integration of predefined algorithms and deep learning methods to support screening in women with dense breast tissue [127,128,129,130].
Both traditional algorithms (using predefined features) and deep learning methods have proven effective in distinguishing malignant lesions. However, combining these approaches or fusion models has shown even better results. In tests across 690 MRI cases, 245 mammograms, and 1,125 ultrasound scans, fusion models outperformed standalone methods, suggesting that blending human-designed features with AI-learned patterns could enhance diagnostic accuracy. This hybrid approach highlights the growing role of AI in supporting precise, data-driven breast cancer assessments [131, 132]. Deep-learning methods have also been recently employed in the classification of breast cancer based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) and image fusion approaches using ultrasonography [133]. AI tools are transforming breast cancer management, offering clearer insights into detection, prognosis, and better treatment outcomes for patients.
3.5.4 Gastric cancer
Gastric cancer ranks fifth in prevalence and fourth in mortality among cancers worldwide. With the advent of AI, machine learning algorithms have been progressively developed and broadly applied to its diagnosis and treatment. Notable applications include survival prediction and neoadjuvant chemotherapy benefit modeling using support vector machines (SVM), lymph node metastasis prediction in early gastric cancer via decision tree (DT) models [134], HER2 status classification using random forest (RF) models [135], artificial neural network-based screening and diagnosis of non-invasive gastric cancer [136], and gastric cancer lymph node metastasis classification through K-nearest neighbors (KNN) algorithms [137].
3.5.5 Kidney cancer
Cross-sectional imaging of kidneys has led to increased detection of renal lesions, followed by increased surgeries and ablations performed for suspected malignant tumors, thereby decreasing patient compliance and increase in healthcare costs. Therefore, a more accurate prediction and identification of benign renal lesions could possibly avoid the invasive nature of surgeries and associated risk and mortality [138]. Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provide an estimate of the probability of malignancy, while percutaneous biopsy is another invasive procedure for identifying the type of tumor in renal lesions, putting the patients at risk of complications such as hemorrhage, infection, and implantation metastasis [139]. This underscores the need for non-invasive diagnostic approaches to characterize benign renal masses and distinguish aggressive tumors requiring immediate intervention from non-cancerous lesions amenable to alternative management strategies.
Thus AI-driven quantitative analysis of preoperative medical images has been utilized recently for patient compliance and better management of cancer treatment. Recently, Xiong et al. (2025) demonstrated that deep learning models can non-invasively estimate the likelihood of malignant and aggressive pathology in renal masses using preoperative multi-phase CT imaging [140].
3.5.6 Lung cancer
Lung cancer carries the highest mortality rate globally [141], with adenocarcinoma being the most prevalent histopathological subtype, accounting for approximately one-third to half of all cases [142]. The integration of AI into digital pathology has enabled quantitative analysis of H&E-stained whole slide images (WSIs) [58], superseding conventional histopathological examination. Pathomics leverages WSIs for high-throughput quantitative extraction of histological and cytological features, facilitating detailed characterization of the tumor microenvironment, for instance, pathomic features have been employed to trace immune and molecular evolution from lung preneoplasia to invasive adenocarcinoma [143, 144]. Deep learning has demonstrated advantages over traditional pathomics by employing specialized neural networks to construct end-to-end classification models, offering greater potential for tumor segmentation, feature extraction, classification, and outcome prediction [145, 146]. The combined application of deep learning and pathomics is currently under investigation for identifying abnormal tumor regions and preliminarily classifying lung cancer invasiveness from pathological sections, with the dual benefit of reducing workload and improving predictive accuracy [147, 148].
3.5.7 Prostate cancer
Prostate cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in men and the fourth most common cause of mortality worldwide [149]. The heterogeneity of this cancer type can lead to a range of outcomes varying from slow-growing, harmless tumors to aggressive cancers resulting in high morbidity and mortality. This variability complicates decisions about treatment planning, prognosis, and prediction of treatment response. To address this, genomic profiling tools have been incorporated into the National Comprehensive Cancer Network Guidelines, including Decipher (GenomeDx Biosciences, San Diego, CA), Oncotype DX Prostate (Genomic Health Inc, Redwood City, CA), and Prolaris (Myriad Genetics Inc, Salt Lake City, UT) [21].
AI not only has the potential for molecular characterization but can also guide clinicians about the management of prostate cancer, including detection, diagnosis, staging, monitoring, and treatment planning for patients. Deep learning networks, and CNNs in particular, have transformed prostate cancer detection and diagnosis by leveraging diverse imaging modalities, network architectures, and training strategies for cancer classification [150, 151].
3.5.8 Skin cancer
Skin cancer is one of the most prevalent cancers and is the 17th most common cancer worldwide [152]. Skin cancer diagnosis typically relies on visual assessment, beginning with clinical screening followed by dermoscopic analysis or biopsy with histopathological examination. Classification and imaging of skin lesions remain challenging due to the inherent variability in normal skin appearance.
3.5.9 Urothelial cancer
Urothelial carcinoma (UC), most commonly arising in the bladder, ranks among the leading malignancies in women and is the fourth most frequent in men. At diagnosis, over 75% of patients have non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), which is manageable with surgery and intravesical therapy, while the remaining 25% harbor muscle-invasive disease necessitating more aggressive intervention such as cystectomy, radiotherapy, or palliative care [153]. Although there has been significant progress in this type of cancer progression and disease management, survival rates are poor. This highlights the critical need for pre-screening diagnostic tools capable of rapidly and cost-effectively identifying patients at high risk of disease progression, while directing those with low-risk profiles straight to appropriate therapy, avoiding unnecessary delays from extensive workup.
Existing pre-clinical testing tools for UC, such as PCR and next-generation sequencing, demand high-quality tissue, involve lengthy turnaround times, and are costly. To address these limitations, Banier et al. (2024) developed a deep learning model for detecting FGFR3 mutations, offering a more rapid and cost-effective pre-screening approach for identifying patients eligible for FGFR3-targeted therapies [154]. This highlights the importance of employing AI in cancer diagnosis and management for a cost-effective treatment strategy.
Novel AI tools of machine learning and deep learning neural networks have paved the path in the detection of skin lesions, skin types, and abnormalities demonstrating enhanced potential for skin lesion classification and cancer detection [155]. Several studies using massive number of datasets of clinical and dermascopic skin images have found AI to be extremely effective in skin cancer classification [156].
3.6 AI in adherence and supportive care of cancer patients
Cancer care is evolving rapidly as treatment moves increasingly into outpatient settings. Many patients now receive oral systemic anticancer therapies (SACT) and manage complex regimens at home, placing greater responsibility on them to take medications correctly, monitor symptoms, and communicate changes promptly. As a result, maintaining strong adherence and delivering timely supportive care have become essential for ensuring treatment effectiveness and quality of life. Between 2020 and 2025, research has expanded quickly in exploring how artificial intelligence (AI) can support these needs. A broad range of AI-enabled tools including predictive risk algorithms, remote patient monitoring systems, chatbots, smart pill dispensers, and ingestible digital sensors have shown promise in identifying adherence challenges, detecting early symptom deterioration, and preventing treatment interruptions. These technologies have been particularly impactful in cancer types commonly managed in ambulatory care, including breast, lung, and colorectal cancers, as well as hematologic malignancies.
A major advancement in this field is the development of AI-driven predictive models capable of identifying patients at high risk for non-adherence or treatment interruption. Machine learning models trained on electronic health records, pharmacy refill histories, socioeconomic factors, comorbidities, and patient-reported outcomes have demonstrated strong predictive performance. These systems help clinicians differentiate between patients likely to follow therapy and those who may require closer monitoring, counseling, or automated reminder tools. For example, a large multi-cancer study found in a real-world study of 152 cancer patients on oral anticancer drugs, about 27% were non-adherent meaning more than a quarter failed to take their medications as prescribed [157]. Recent study showed that13 randomized controlled trials found that digital AI intervention users had a significantly lower risk of poor adherence to oral systemic anticancer therapy than non-users (Odds Ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.47–0.77). These digital tools significantly improved adherence metrics compared with standard care [158].
Traditional approaches rely on periodic clinical visits and static treatment protocols that may not reflect dynamic patient needs. AI-based systems, using reinforcement learning and predictive modeling, can analyze real-time patient data to recommend personalized medication modifications. This flexibility allows treatment plans to shift proactively with changes in patient status, improving therapeutic outcomes and reducing the likelihood of adverse effects. Continuous monitoring further enhances timely intervention [159]. Wearable devices and digital health platforms supply ongoing physiological and behavioral data, enabling early detection of deviations from expected health patterns. When AI systems recognize signs of deterioration or lapses in adherence, they can trigger alerts for clinicians or patients, helping prevent complications and reducing emergency visits [160].
AI-enabled remote patient monitoring (RPM) and electronic patient-reported outcomes (ePROs) have also proven effective in detecting symptoms early and reducing emergency care utilization. Randomized trials and real-world studies show that ePRO systems with automated alerts or triage algorithms prompt earlier intervention, lower emergency visit rates, and improve symptom control in lung, breast, and gastrointestinal cancers [161, 162]. Another fast-growing area is AI-driven chatbots, which offer around-the-clock support for patients navigating complex regimens. Tools such as Florence, Medi Reminder, Conferbot, and Sensely provide medication reminders, guide symptom self-management, and offer psychosocial support [163]. These tools are especially useful for breast cancer survivors on long-term endocrine therapy, lung cancer patients with variable symptoms, and individuals with hematologic malignancies requiring ongoing reassurance.
Despite these advances, challenges remain as predictive models often lack external validation and may not generalize across diverse cancer populations. Additionally, adherence measurement varies widely from self-report to refill data to sensor-based systems making comparisons difficult [164]. Therefore, while AI holds strong potential to enhance adherence and supportive care, it should not replace human-centered care. Further research is needed to address issues related to privacy, personalization, and long-term effectiveness.
