5 Prospects and challenges: responsible AI governance
The integration of AI in cancer management has enabled the development of predictive models for identifying high-risk individuals, supporting early detection, improving lesion characterization, and informing treatment planning. AI-driven classification and differentiation of cancer types may also support more tailored treatment strategies, while advanced algorithms have shown potential in tumor-lesion characterization, assessment of growth patterns, and prediction of treatment response. However, the clinical impact of these models varies substantially across datasets, algorithms, cancer types, and implementation settings. While some AI tools have shown real-world promise, many remain at the retrospective-development or proof-of-concept stage. Demonstrating actual improvements in patient outcomes, survival, workflow efficiency, and health equity requires prospective validation, external testing, transparent reporting, and post-deployment monitoring [4].
5.1 Critical limitations of deep learning models in cancer imaging and prediction
Although deep learning models have shown considerable promise in cancer imaging, histopathology, radiomics, and clinical prediction, their limitations require careful interpretation, particularly before clinical implementation [168]. A major concern is generalizability, as deep learning algorithms developed for radiologic diagnosis often show reduced performance when tested on external datasets rather than only on internal validation cohorts. Models trained on retrospectively collected or single-institution datasets may capture dataset-specific patterns instead of robust disease-related features [169]. In histopathology, for example, variations in staining and color appearance between laboratories can affect convolutional neural network performance, making stain normalization and augmentation important for improving model robustness [170]. Similarly, in radiomics, differences in image acquisition, segmentation, and processing can reduce feature repeatability and reproducibility across studies [171]. As a result, strong internal validation performance may not translate into equivalent performance across external hospitals, imaging devices, patient populations, or clinical workflows [169]. This issue is particularly important in oncology, where tumor heterogeneity, image-acquisition variability, and differences in tumor segmentation or annotation can substantially influence model behavior [172].
Importantly, high diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, or AUC values reported in AI studies should be interpreted in light of study design and dataset construction. Many cancer imaging and prediction models are developed using retrospective datasets, internally curated image collections, or selected cases with confirmed diagnoses and relatively complete metadata. Such datasets may exclude poor-quality images, diagnostically ambiguous cases, rare subtypes, incomplete records, or technically challenging scans that are frequently encountered in routine clinical practice. In addition, internal validation strategies may not adequately test performance across different institutions, scanners, imaging protocols, patient populations, or clinical workflows. These factors can produce overly optimistic estimates of model performance and may exaggerate apparent clinical readiness. Therefore, strong performance on retrospective or internally validated datasets should be considered hypothesis-generating unless supported by independent external validation, prospective evaluation, and transparent reporting of dataset selection, exclusions, preprocessing, and validation procedures [84, 85, 169, 173].
Real-world implementation also requires validation across geographically and demographically distinct cohorts. AI models trained in one country, institution, or healthcare system may not maintain the same performance across borders because of differences in patient demographics, genetic ancestry, cancer prevalence, comorbidity patterns, screening practices, imaging equipment, acquisition protocols, annotation conventions, referral pathways, treatment standards, and healthcare infrastructure. External validation is therefore essential for assessing whether model performance is robust beyond the original development setting. A systematic review of externally validated deep-learning algorithms for radiologic diagnosis found that published external validation studies remain relatively infrequent and that most externally tested algorithms showed reduced performance on external datasets compared with internal validation datasets [169]. These findings are consistent with broader concerns in cancer imaging AI, where dataset heterogeneity, institutional variation, and limited external validation remain major barriers to clinical translation [21]. Future oncology AI studies should therefore prioritize multicenter and, where possible, multinational validation, together with subgroup analyses across age, sex, ethnicity, geography, socioeconomic status, cancer subtype, and healthcare setting. Without such validation, AI tools risk performing unevenly across populations and may unintentionally worsen existing disparities in cancer diagnosis and treatment.
Another important failure mode is data leakage, in which information from the training dataset unintentionally influences model validation or testing. Leakage may occur through patient-level overlap between training and test sets, image slices from the same patient being split across different datasets, preprocessing performed before dataset separation, or repeated use of the test set during model tuning. Such leakage can artificially inflate accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, or AUC and may create an exaggerated impression of clinical readiness [173].
Overfitting is another major challenge in medical imaging AI. Deep learning models often contain a very large number of trainable parameters, while medical imaging datasets are frequently limited in size, imbalanced, or enriched for selected cases. Under these conditions, models may memorize dataset-specific features rather than learn robust diagnostic representations. Overfitting is especially likely when model development lacks patient-level data splitting, external validation, adequate cross-validation, or transparent reporting of hyperparameter tuning. In medical image segmentation, Renard et al. noted that dataset sampling, validation strategy, architecture choice, optimization, and implementation differences can all contribute to variability and poor reproducibility of deep learning results [174].
Reproducibility also remains a persistent concern. Many AI studies do not fully report dataset characteristics, preprocessing steps, augmentation methods, model architecture, hyperparameters, code availability, computing environment, or statistical uncertainty around performance estimates. These omissions make it difficult for independent researchers to replicate findings or compare models fairly. In one review of deep learning segmentation studies, only a small proportion of articles provided enough methodological information to allow full reproducibility, and source-code availability was limited [175]. Therefore, future studies in AI-based cancer management should follow transparent reporting frameworks such as CLAIM for medical imaging AI and TRIPOD + AI for clinical prediction models. CLAIM 2024 was developed to improve transparency and reproducibility in medical imaging AI research, while TRIPOD + AI provides updated reporting guidance for prediction models using regression or machine-learning methods [176, 177].
5.2 Data infrastructure, annotation, and interoperability challenges
The clinical implementation of AI in cancer imaging depends strongly on the availability of standardized, interoperable, and well-curated medical data. Existing digital imaging infrastructures provide an important foundation for this process. Picture Archiving and Communication Systems (PACS) enable the digital acquisition, storage, transmission, retrieval, and display of medical images, supporting the transition from film-based radiology to integrated digital imaging workflows [178]. Similarly, Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) serves as the international standard for the communication and management of medical imaging information and related data, facilitating interoperability among imaging devices, workstations, storage systems, and clinical software [179].
However, the availability of digital imaging data alone does not ensure that such data are ready for AI development or clinical deployment. AI models require datasets that are accurately labelled, consistently annotated, appropriately segmented, and accompanied by reliable metadata and quality-control procedures. In oncology, these requirements are particularly demanding because tumor boundaries, lesion characteristics, disease stage, treatment response, and outcome labels often require expert interpretation by radiologists, pathologists, oncologists, or multidisciplinary teams. Poor annotation quality, inconsistent segmentation, scanner variability, image artefacts, limited dataset diversity, and single-center data collection can reduce model reliability and limit generalizability across institutions and patient populations [180, 181].
Therefore, future AI development in cancer management should prioritize not only larger datasets but also better-curated, representative, and multicenter datasets. Standardized image acquisition, harmonized annotation protocols, quality assurance procedures, and secure data-sharing frameworks are essential to reduce dataset bias and improve reproducibility. Improved access to well-documented public and collaborative datasets may also support external validation and fairer comparison of AI models across different clinical settings.
5.3 Ethical governance of clinical data and medical records
The use of clinical files, electronic health records, imaging archives, pathology reports, genomic profiles, and other medical records for AI model development require clear ethical governance before data extraction, model training, and secondary research use. Ethical review committees or institutional review boards should evaluate whether the proposed AI study has scientific and clinical justification, whether the data requested are proportionate to the research objective, and whether appropriate safeguards are in place for privacy, confidentiality, bias reduction, and responsible data use. The World Health Organization emphasizes that AI for health should be guided by ethical principles including autonomy, human oversight, transparency, accountability, inclusiveness, equity, responsiveness, and sustainable public interest [182].
Patient privacy is particularly important in oncology because AI models may integrate highly sensitive information, including diagnostic images, pathology slides, genetic or molecular data, treatment history, survival outcomes, and longitudinal follow-up records. Therefore, training datasets should be governed by data-minimization principles, de-identification or anonymization where appropriate, secure access control, audit trails, and clear data-use agreements. Where identifiable or re-identifiable data are used, informed consent, consent waiver procedures, or other legally and ethically approved governance mechanisms should be clearly defined. Patient perspectives research also suggests that patients may expect disclosure when AI tools are used in diagnosis and may want understandable information on the AI system’s purpose, risks, and role in care [183].
Archival digitalization standards are also essential for safe and reproducible AI development. In imaging-based oncology, DICOM provides the international standard for transmitting, storing, retrieving, processing, and displaying medical imaging information, enabling interoperability among imaging devices, PACS, workstations, archives, and clinical software [184]. For broader clinical records, Health Level 7 (HL7) Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) is widely used to represent and exchange electronic health information and supports interoperability across health information systems [185]. Standardized archiving, metadata curation, version control, and secure digital infrastructure are therefore necessary to ensure that clinical records used for AI training are traceable, interoperable, quality-controlled, and ethically governed.
5.4 Explainability and clinical interpretability
Explainability is a central requirement for the clinical adoption of AI in oncology because clinicians must be able to understand, question, and contextualize algorithmic outputs before applying them in patient care [186]. In cancer imaging and prediction, explainable AI can strengthen clinician trust by showing which image regions, radiomic features, or clinical variables contributed to a model’s prediction [187]. This is especially important in high-stakes tasks such as tumor detection, lesion segmentation, risk stratification, and treatment-response prediction, where unexplained outputs may limit accountability, clinical judgment, and professional acceptance [188]. Explainability is also important from ethical, legal, and patient-centered perspectives, as opaque AI systems may affect autonomy, responsibility, safety, trust, informed consent, and liability in clinical care [186].
Recent work has moved beyond single heatmap-based explanations toward hybrid and multi-level explainable AI (XAI) approaches. For example, Gagliardi et al. proposed BrAInVision, a hybrid explainable AI framework for brain MRI analysis that integrates deep learning with traditional machine-learning features. The framework combines visual explanations through Grad-CAM with feature-level interpretation using permutation feature importance and partial dependence plots, providing both local visual interpretability and broader insight into model behavior. Such approaches are valuable in medical imaging because they allow clinicians to compare model attention with anatomically meaningful regions while also assessing the contribution of quantitative image features [189].
Nevertheless, XAI should not be viewed as a substitute for rigorous validation. Explanations may appear convincing while still being incomplete, unstable, or misleading if the model has learned confounding patterns, shortcut features, scanner-specific artifacts, or dataset biases [190]. Therefore, explainability should be assessed alongside external validation, calibration, subgroup performance, clinical plausibility, and workflow testing [191]. In this context, XAI is best understood as part of a broader framework for transparent, accountable, and clinically responsible AI deployment rather than simply as a tool for making AI outputs more acceptable [191].
5.5 Hybrid AI models as an emerging direction in cancer imaging
In addition to end-to-end deep learning, hybrid AI models are increasingly important in cancer imaging because they combine complementary information from automatically learned features, handcrafted radiomics, pathomics, clinical variables, and conventional machine-learning classifiers [192]. Handcrafted radiomics features, such as shape, intensity, and texture descriptors, provide quantitative and relatively interpretable image information, whereas deep learning can capture complex spatial and hierarchical patterns that may be difficult to define manually [193]. Integrating both feature types may therefore improve model robustness, interpretability, and clinical relevance, especially when imaging datasets are limited or heterogeneous [194]. However, oncological radiomics still requires careful harmonization, multicenter validation, and transparent reporting because feature extraction, preprocessing, segmentation, and scanner variability can strongly influence model performance [171].
Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) is another important weakly supervised strategy, particularly in digital pathology and whole-slide image analysis. Whole-slide images are gigapixel-scale tissue images, making detailed pixel-level or patch-level annotation time-consuming, costly, and difficult to standardize across pathology laboratories. MIL addresses this challenge by treating each whole-slide image as a “bag” of smaller patches or instances and learning diagnostically relevant regions from slide-level labels. This is especially useful in oncology, where slide-level diagnostic labels are often available from routine pathology reports, while detailed region-level annotations may not be available [195].
Clinically, MIL has been applied to cancer detection, tumor subtype classification, histological grading, biomarker prediction, lymph-node metastasis detection, and prognostic modelling using whole-slide pathology images. Attention-based MIL approaches can also highlight tissue regions that contribute most strongly to a slide-level prediction, thereby offering a degree of interpretability and helping pathologists assess whether model attention corresponds to biologically meaningful tumor areas. Although outside oncology, similar MIL principles have also been applied to diabetic retinopathy image classification, supporting the broader relevance of weakly supervised learning in medical imaging tasks where diagnostically important abnormalities may occupy only small localized regions of larger images [196].
Despite these advantages, MIL models have important limitations. Their performance can be influenced by tissue preprocessing, staining variability, scanner differences, patch extraction strategy, magnification level, bag size, pooling method, and the quality of slide-level labels. Attention maps may also be misleading if the model learns artifacts, background tissue, or institution-specific features rather than true disease biology. In addition, MIL models often require large and diverse training cohorts, independent external validation, and careful assessment across different laboratories, scanners, tissue-processing protocols, and patient populations before they can be considered clinically reliable [197].
A recent example of a hybrid and explainable architecture is MultiExCam, developed for skin lesion classification. It integrates dermatoscopic images, deep-learning-derived features, and handcrafted statistical features within an ensemble architecture using gating and attention mechanisms. The model also incorporates gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) to highlight relevant image regions and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to explain feature contributions, demonstrating how hybrid AI can move beyond purely black-box classification by combining prediction with interpretable evidence [198]. Nevertheless, as with other medical AI systems, such models should be interpreted cautiously until their performance is confirmed through external validation, prospective testing, and evaluation across diverse clinical populations and imaging settings [199].
5.6 Federated learning and privacy-preserving AI frameworks
Federated learning is an increasingly important approach for multicenter oncology AI because it enables collaborative model training across institutions without requiring the direct transfer of raw patient data. Instead of pooling imaging, pathology, genomic, or clinical records into a central repository, participating centers train models locally and share model parameters or updates for aggregation. This structure is particularly relevant in cancer research, where datasets often contain highly sensitive information, including diagnostic images, whole-slide pathology images, genomic profiles, treatment history, and survival outcomes. By keeping data within the originating institution, federated learning may help address institutional data-sharing barriers, privacy concerns, and cross-border restrictions while still allowing models to learn from larger and more diverse patient populations [200, 201].
In oncology imaging, federated learning has already demonstrated practical value. For example, a large glioblastoma study trained a tumor boundary detection model using data from 71 sites across 6 continents without centralizing patient data, showing improved tumor delineation compared with a model trained on publicly available data alone [198]. Federated approaches have also been explored in histopathology image analysis, where collaborative training can improve model performance while reducing the need to transfer sensitive whole-slide images between institutions [202]. Similarly, privacy-preserving federated methods are increasingly relevant for omics and genomic data, where re-identification risks and legal restrictions make centralized data sharing particularly challenging [203].
However, federated learning should not be viewed as a complete privacy solution on its own. Model updates or gradients may still leak sensitive information if appropriate safeguards are not used. Therefore, privacy-preserving AI frameworks may combine federated learning with additional techniques such as secure aggregation, differential privacy, encrypted computation, access control, audit trails, and clear data-governance agreements. These safeguards are important for protecting patient confidentiality while enabling multicenter validation and model development. At the same time, federated learning introduces practical challenges, including heterogeneous imaging protocols, unequal dataset sizes across institutions, variable annotation quality, communication costs, cybersecurity risks, and difficulty monitoring model bias across participating sites. Therefore, future oncology AI studies using federated learning should report participating-site characteristics, aggregation methods, privacy safeguards, validation strategies, subgroup performance, and governance procedures transparently [202, 203].
Several other emerging technical pathways may further strengthen the clinical translation of AI in cancer management. Large language models may also support oncology workflows by assisting with clinical documentation, extraction of information from electronic health records, literature summarization, patient-facing communication, and decision-support tasks, although their outputs require careful validation for accuracy, bias, privacy, and safety [204, 205]. In parallel, explainable AI can improve clinical trust by helping clinicians understand which image regions, features, or variables contributed to model predictions. Future AI systems may also increasingly integrate digital pathology with spatial transcriptomics, allowing morphological tissue patterns to be linked with spatially resolved molecular information and tumor microenvironment heterogeneity [206, 207]. These pathways suggest that the next phase of AI in oncology will likely move beyond isolated prediction models toward privacy-preserving, multimodal, explainable, and biologically informed systems for precision cancer care.
5.7 Ethical, regulatory, and implementation considerations
Responsible integration of AI into oncology requires ethical, regulatory, and implementation frameworks that address patient safety, clinical accountability, privacy, transparency, bias, and post-deployment performance. AI-based tools used for diagnosis, prognosis, treatment planning, or clinical decision support can influence high-stakes medical decisions. Therefore, they should be assessed not only for technical accuracy but also for generalizability, robustness, calibration, clinical usefulness, and subgroup performance [208]. In oncology, these concerns are particularly important because AI outputs may influence decisions regarding biopsy, surgery, radiotherapy, systemic therapy, treatment sequencing, surveillance intensity, palliative care referral, and clinical trial eligibility. AI-based decision-making in oncology has been associated with ethical and legal concerns related to informed consent, accountability, transparency, clinician responsibility, and patient trust [209]. Legal and clinical accountability becomes especially complex when AI-generated recommendations conflict with established clinical guidelines, multidisciplinary tumor board decisions, or clinician judgment. In such cases, AI outputs should not be treated as autonomous directives; rather, the treating clinician and institution should retain responsibility for determining whether a recommendation is guideline-consistent, biologically plausible, clinically appropriate, and aligned with patient preferences. This is consistent with broader discussions of clinical AI, where opacity and uncertain allocation of responsibility remain major concerns in AI-assisted decision-making [210].
AI-based prognostic tools also require careful ethical handling in cancer care. Survival predictions, recurrence-risk estimates, or treatment-response probabilities may support shared decision-making, but they may also influence patient anxiety, expectations, hope, and willingness to accept treatment if communicated without adequate clinical context. Prognostic communication in cancer care is already recognized as difficult, and the optimal method for presenting prognostic information to support patient understanding, psychological adjustment, and decision-making remains uncertain [211]. Therefore, AI-generated prognostic outputs should be presented as probabilistic and context-dependent rather than deterministic. Clinicians should explain the uncertainty, limitations, and intended use of such predictions, particularly in advanced cancer or palliative settings where prognostic information may influence goals-of-care discussions and treatment preferences. Evidence from palliative oncology further supports the need for careful, patient-centered prognostic communication [212].
Regulatory oversight is particularly important for AI/ML-based software as a medical device because such systems may be updated after deployment and may show changing performance in real-world clinical settings. Peer-reviewed regulatory analyses emphasize the need for lifecycle-based oversight, transparency, good machine-learning practice, and real-world performance monitoring for AI/ML-enabled medical technologies [213]. Recent journal literature on Predetermined Change Control Plans further highlights the importance of supporting iterative improvement in AI-enabled devices while maintaining safety, effectiveness, and regulatory compliance [214].
In clinical oncology, regulatory evaluation should consider the model’s intended use, training data, external validation, calibration, subgroup performance, explainability, cybersecurity, human oversight, and post-market monitoring. These requirements are especially relevant for adaptive or continuously updated AI systems, where performance may shift after deployment because of changes in patient populations, imaging protocols, clinical workflows, software updates, or real-world data distributions [215]. For such systems, regulatory evaluation should include version control, audit trails, predefined update boundaries, documentation of model changes, and continuous real-world performance monitoring to ensure that iterative updates do not compromise safety or clinical reliability. FDA guidance on Predetermined Change Control Plans similarly emphasizes that planned modifications to AI-enabled devices should support iterative improvement while maintaining reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness [216]. Ethical implementation also requires clear responsibility for AI-assisted decisions, protection of patient confidentiality, informed clinician use, and transparent communication about the strengths and limitations of AI outputs. Ultimately, AI should be implemented as a decision-support tool that complements clinical expertise rather than replacing professional judgment [217].
6 Conclusion
AI is increasingly shaping cancer management by supporting image-based detection, tumor characterization, histopathological assessment, genomic interpretation, prognostic modelling, treatment-response prediction, and clinical decision support. The reviewed evidence suggests that AI is most mature in image-based detection, classification, and segmentation tasks, while applications involving survival prediction, molecular characterization, treatment selection, and real-time clinical decision support require stronger validation before routine implementation. Despite its promise, the clinical readiness of AI tools remains uneven. Many models are limited by retrospective study designs, heterogeneous datasets, insufficient external validation, data leakage risks, overfitting, limited explainability, and uncertain reproducibility across real-world settings. Future progress will therefore depend on transparent reporting, diverse multicenter datasets, standardized annotation, hybrid and explainable modelling approaches, regulatory oversight, and post-deployment monitoring. AI should ultimately be viewed as a decision-support framework that complements clinical expertise and strengthens precision oncology when supported by rigorous validation and responsible governance.

title: The enduring appeal of Vietnam’s sidewalk coffee
content:
Vietnamese people have long gathered in public spaces to drink tea, chat, and observe the world around them.
From house verandas and village tea stalls to street-side tea shops, a cup of tea has never been just about quenching thirst.
It has also been an excuse to meet, exchange stories, catch up on local news or simply sit and take in the rhythm of everyday life.
Tea once held a particularly important place in Vietnamese culture.
In his celebrated 1940 short-story collection Vang bong mot thoi (Echoes of a Bygone Time), renowned Vietnamese writer Nguyen Tuan portrayed tea drinking as an art, complete with its own rituals and cultural traditions.
As urbanization and social life evolved, another drink gradually found its way into the lives of city dwellers, creating a culture of its own: coffee.
Humble setting, exceptional coffee
Calling it 'sidewalk coffee' does not imply inferior coffee, poor service, or a casual approach to the drinking experience.
Beyond those assumptions, sidewalk coffee has become a distinctive part of Hanoi’s urban culture, shaped in part by its long-standing tea-drinking traditions.
It does not necessarily mean coffee served in dusty or makeshift surroundings. It can be found on clean, open sidewalks by lakes, along city streets, or beneath tree-lined roads.
Summer brings the crimson blooms of flamboyant trees, while autumn carries the faint scent of frangipani through the breeze, against a backdrop of women in elegant, traditional Vietnamese ao dai.
City dwellers come to sidewalk cafés to savor coffee that is bitter, sweet, rich and fragrant while taking in the constant flow of life around them.
Familiar sounds, voices calling out, motorbike engines and vendors selling tofu pudding, sticky rice and sweet soups, become part of the rhythm of everyday life.
Some watch each drop of coffee slowly fall, letting the passing minutes inspire quiet, reflective thoughts.
Others come to listen to friends’ conversations and banter, picking up new bits of information and perspectives along the way.
The habit of observing the world around them is not unique to coffee drinkers.
It may also reflect a broader trait shaped by Vietnam’s traditional agricultural culture, in which people have long lived closely connected to their surroundings.
Sidewalk coffee, then, is not simply about an affordable cup of coffee. It is an unpretentious style of socializing open to everyone, regardless of status.
A sidewalk café offers a modest, easygoing social space without the flashiness or pretension found elsewhere.
Each customer comes for their own reasons, following their own tastes and looking to connect with others.
Often, the coffee and the sidewalk are simply an excuse to sit down, talk, share personal stories or discuss whatever has caught their attention.
Coffee, conversation, and everything in between
Vietnam’s diverse regional cultures are reflected in the conversations that unfold over coffee, which can range from politics and business to culture and sports, both at home and around the world.
Sometimes, the conversation turns to business, with deals discussed and settled quickly, efficiently and with a distinctly businesslike air.
The atmosphere becomes even livelier when groups of writers, intellectuals or students gather for a chat. No topic is off limits, and all kinds of issues are brought up and debated.
Every now and then, someone carried away by the moment may even recite a few gentle, lyrical lines of 'luc bat,' Vietnam’s traditional six-eight verse form.
This may partly explain why sidewalk cafés tend to have a different atmosphere from beer halls or drinking spots, with fewer arguments and raised voices.
The setting is simple: a few small plastic or wooden stools, a menu of hot or iced coffee, perhaps some peanut candy and a few cigarettes.
Regardless of who they are, a successful businessperson, an overseas Vietnamese, a government official, a manual laborer, a factory worker or a shoe shiner, customers sit in the same kind of space and are offered much the same menu.
That natural sense of equality is enough to give sidewalk coffee its distinctive character, without the need for expensive, upscale restaurants.
Coffee culture has become such an ordinary and natural part of daily life that meeting a friend or business partner often begins with a familiar invitation: “Let’s grab a coffee.”
If language is a tool for expressing how people think, this everyday phrase may also reveal something about the way coffee is woven into Vietnamese culture.
Vietnamese coffee is typically brewed strong rather than diluted, unlike coffee in many other parts of the world.
That preference may stem partly from Vietnam’s regional climate and partly from the long-standing habit of drinking strong tea.
Together, these influences may have helped shape a Vietnamese temperament that is assertive and decisive, yet also measured and restrained.
By definition, sidewalk coffee takes place along streets with sidewalks, so the culture has flourished mainly in major cities such as Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, and Nha Trang.
It tends to thrive where tradition and modern life intersect, among people who appreciate coffee and value the simple, authentic and beautiful things in life.
Today, no Vietnamese writer has elevated coffee, or sidewalk coffee in particular, into a way of its own, as writer Nguyen Tuan once did with tea.
Yet coffee may have already become part of the cultural fabric of many Hanoians.
To understand that spirit, one place to start is with a cup of sidewalk coffee.

title: Entregan permisos para cremar al preso político José Breijo tras dos meses
content:
Entregan permisos para cremar al preso político José Breijo tras dos meses
La Fiscalía 140 de Caracas y el Cicpc autorizaron la entrega y cremación de los restos del preso político venezolano-uruguayo José Breijo a casi dos meses de su deceso. El activista Carlos Julio Rojas atribuyó el dictamen a la presión de organizaciones sociales y denunció tratos crueles e irregularidades durante el periodo de reclusión de la víctima.
La Fiscalía 140 del Área Metropolitana de Caracas y el Cuerpo de Investigaciones Científicas, Penales y Criminalísticas (Cicpc) emitieron la autorización legal para proceder a la entrega y cremación de los restos del preso político de nacionalidad venezolana y uruguaya José Breijo, casi dos meses después de su fallecimiento bajo custodia.
El anuncio fue difundido por el coordinador del Frente Norte de Caracas y activista de derechos humanos, Carlos Julio Rojas, quien atribuyó la obtención de la orden judicial al seguimiento de las organizaciones civiles, familiares y medios de comunicación. Rojas detalló que la solicitud para retirar el cuerpo de la sede del Servicio Nacional de Medicina y Ciencias Forenses (Senamecf) se ejecutará este lunes con el aval de Santiago Breijo, familiar del fallecido.
Durante la publicación de un mensaje en sus redes sociales, el dirigente denunció las condiciones de reclusión a las que fue sometido Breijo, señalando episodios de invasión a su propiedad privada, suspensión de garantías fundamentales y sometimiento a tratos crueles e inhumanos durante el tiempo que permaneció privado de libertad.
«Esto no puede seguir ocurriendo en Venezuela, la violación de derechos humanos. Sufrió tratos crueles e inhumanos, le invadieron su casa y pasaron dos meses para que pudiéramos tener la constancia y el permiso para poder rendirle honores», declaró el activista, al tiempo que ratificó que las cenizas serán esparcidas en el mar, conforme a la voluntad expresada por el ciudadano antes de su deceso.
Las organizaciones defensoras de derechos humanos anunciaron que en los próximos días informarán la fecha y el lugar donde se realizarán los actos de homenaje a Breijo, cuyo caso ha sido calificado por las plataformas civiles como emblemático respecto al tratamiento recibido por los detenidos por causas políticas en el país.
*El periodismo en Venezuela se ejerce en un entorno hostil para la prensa con decenas de instrumentos jurídicos dispuestos para el castigo de la palabra, especialmente las leyes «contra el odio», «contra el fascismo» y «contra el bloqueo». Este contenido fue escrito tomando en consideración las amenazas y límites que, en consecuencia, se han impuesto a la divulgación de informaciones desde dentro del país.

title: Erlösung am Amstettner Hauptplatz: Neuer Pächter für Stadtbrauhof
content: Nach der überraschenden Sperre des Stadtbrauhofs mitten am Amstettner Hauptplatz aufgrund einer Insolvenz im vergangenen Juli kommt nun die erlösende Nachricht. Das erfolgreiche Wirteehepaar Daniela und Dieter Hanusch hat für den 8. bis 10. Oktober die Eröffnungstage in dem stadteigenen Gasthof angekündigt. Bereits gestreute Gerüchte über die neuen Pächter wurden nun bestätigt.Rückkehr in den StadtbrauhofDieter Hanusch kehrt damit an seine langjährige Wirkungsstätte zurück. Bei Wirt Herbert Houska, der den Stadtbrauhof über Jahrzehnte erfolgreich betrieb, war Küchenchef Hanusch eine Stütze des Betriebs.„Der Stadtbrauhof sperrt wieder auf – mit einem Angebot für alle Feinspitze“, bezieht sich Amstettens Bürgermeister und Eigentümersprecher Christian Haberhauer erleichtert auf das Lokal „Der Feinspitz“, das das Ehepaar Hanusch im Fischlmeyergassl, einer Seitengasse des Hauptplatzes, derzeit noch führt.Vom kleinen Feinschmeckerlokal geht’s nun für das Ehepaar Hanusch in die größere Kategorie mit 250 Sitzplätzen und einem großen, zentralen Gastgarten.Küchenklassiker„Feine Schmankerl, faire Preise, Gastfreundschaft und Geselligkeit – einfach richtig gut gemeinsam Essen. Dafür steht der Stadtbrauhof. Mit Dieter Hanusch haben wir hier einen idealen Partner gefunden, der die österreichische Wirtshauskultur aufleben lässt“, ist Stadtchef Haberhauer ganz euphorisch.Klassische Stadtbrauhofgerichte wie Gulasch, Bratwürstel, Bratl, Blunz’ngröstl oder Käsespätzle erwarten die Gäste ebenso wie die gewohnte Feinspitzkarte, die man bislang im Fischlmeyergassl ums Eck gewohnt war.Gestartet wird im Oktober mit Wildwochen, kündigt Dieter Hanusch an. Die Öffnungszeiten werden von Montag bis Samstag sein. Geöffnet ist ab 10 Uhr mit durchgehend warmer Küche ab Mittag.In FünfsternhäusernDieter Hanusch ist 54 Jahre alt. Nach seiner Lehre als Koch in Neuhofen/Ybbs sammelte er erste Erfahrungen in einigen der renommiertesten Saisonbetriebe Österreichs. Während seiner Arbeit in exklusiven Fünfsternhotels verfeinerte er sein Handwerk und entwickelte seinen eigenen Stil.Die Liebe führte ihn 2001 schließlich zurück nach Amstetten in den Stadtbrauhof. Vor drei Jahren wagte er den Schritt in die Selbstständigkeit mit dem erfolgreichen „Feinspitz“.

title: Sex is safe in type 1 diabetes, shows small study using continuous glucose monitoring devices
content:
New research to be presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2, shows, with the use of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) devices, that sexual intercourse is safe for people living with type 1 diabetes. The study is by Dr. Dominica Orłowska, Medical University of Warsaw, Warsaw, Poland, and colleagues.
Sexual intercourse (SI)—as an activity that can consume high levels of energy across various time periods—may be perceived as a risk factor for hypoglycemia (dangerously low blood sugar) by individuals with diabetes, and hypoglycemia-related fear can adversely affect intimacy and quality of life.
The authors explain that when they started asking their patients directly about fear of hypoglycemia during sex, patients said it does happen. There is also some published evidence: In a survey of 53 young adults with type 1 diabetes, approximately one-third reported fear of hypoglycemia during sexual intercourse. But importantly, all the existing evidence comes from questionnaires and interviews. Blood sugar has never before been measured objectively in this context.
Dr. Orłowska explains, "On the one hand, sex is physical exertion like any other and can lower glucose in the same way. But in practice, it is different, and our patients tell us so. Exercise can be planned for—you can reduce your insulin dose, eat beforehand, set an activity mode on your pump.
"Yet sexual activity is usually spontaneous, and it typically happens in the evening or at night, which is already the window of greatest risk for severe and unrecognized hypoglycemia. And above all, nobody talks about it: Patients will discuss exercise with their diabetologist and receive concrete advice, but almost no one asks about sex, so the fear is never addressed. Yet sex life is central to quality of life, and fear of hypoglycemia can lead people to avoid intimacy."
In this research, the authors aimed to assess whether sex is associated with an increased risk of hypoglycemia in adults with T1D based on CGM data.
The study assessed 12 adults with T1D (seven women, five men; median age 36 years, range 21–64 years; mean BMI 24 kg/m²) using CGM (FreeStyle Libre 2 or Guardian 4) who were enrolled in a prospective observational study. Participants were treated with multiple daily injections of insulin (n=6) or insulin pump therapy (n=6; including two using automated insulin delivery systems). None of the five male participants reported erectile dysfunction.
Over a three-month period, participants marked SI events in their CGM application. CGM data collected from 2 hours before to 6 hours after each SI event were analyzed. Subgroup analyses assessed the effects of SI timing (daytime 6 a.m.–8 p.m. vs. nighttime 8 p.m.–6 a.m.), BMI (under 25 versus 25 and over), diabetes duration and insulin delivery mode.
A total of 110 SI events were recorded. All participants using insulin pump therapy reported removing their devices during SI. No clinically significant hypoglycemia was observed. Blood sugar changes were unrelated to insulin therapy mode or diabetes duration.
In 64 events (58%), mean post-SI glucose decreased by 27% (180 to 132 mg/dL; statistically significant); in the remaining 46 events (42%), glucose increased by 34% (122 to 164 mg/dL; statistically significant). Both patterns—increasing and decreasing blood glucose—were observed in SI events in every participant.
Higher pre-SI glucose was associated with a greater post-SI reduction when glucose was decreasing and with a smaller rise when it was increasing. Nighttime SI (66 events) was associated with a statistically significant reduction in glucose levels (165 to 147 mg/dL), whereas daytime SI (n=44) had no effect (144 to 143 mg/dL). There were no differences between mean glucose recorded at 2 and 6 hours after SI.
Participants in the higher BMI group (25 and over) showed a greater post-SI glucose decrease (−10.7%; 150 to 134 mg/dL; statistically significant) than those with BMI under 25 (−5.6%; 159 to 150 mg/dL; not statistically significant).
The authors conclude, "Sexual intercourse in adults with T1D does not appear to increase the risk of clinically significant hypoglycemia, even at night. Blood sugar responses are bidirectional and seem to be influenced by pre-SI glucose level, BMI and time of day. These findings may support clinical counseling and help reduce hypoglycemia-fear-related avoidance of sexual activity in people living with T1D."
They add a cautionary note about people with T1D not using CGM, explaining, "In an ideal world, every person with type 1 diabetes should be using CGM. Those who do not may have no idea whether they are experiencing hypoglycemia during sex—or, in fact, in any setting."

title: Your Parent Keeps Repeating the Same Story? 7 Things You Can Do to Keep Their Brain Active
content: There's a specific kind of moment a lot of us are living through right now. You're on a video call with your parents, half scrolling, when your mother tells you a story. The same one she told you last Sunday. You smile, don't mention it. Later that week, your father misplaces his glasses for the third time this month, and it becomes a joke in the family group chat. Then there's the pause. The one where your mum is mid-sentence, reaching for a word, and it just doesn't come. She laughs, says her memory isn't what it used to be, and moves on. So do you. We're trained to read all of this as nothing, just what happens when people get older. And to be fair, most of the time, that's exactly what it is. Brains slow down with age the same way knees get creakier and eyesight gets weaker; a repeated story or a misplaced pair of glasses isn't a diagnosis, and it doesn't mean Alzheimer's is waiting around the corner. But doctors who specialise in ageing brains say there's a real difference between this ordinary, everyday forgetfulness and the kind that actually signals something more serious. And not knowing where that line is, is exactly what costs families the years when help would have mattered most. So what actually is Alzheimer's? To answer that, it helps to know what Alzheimer's actually is, and how it's different from your parents just having an off day. Ageing can bring everyday forgetfulness, but it does not make memory loss inevitable. Photograph: (India Currents) Alzheimer's is the most common form of dementia, a broader term for a decline in memory, thinking and reasoning severe enough to disrupt daily life. It happens when abnormal protein deposits build up in the brain and gradually damage the connections between nerve cells, usually starting with short-term memory before affecting language, judgement and, eventually, basic daily tasks. It isn't a normal part of ageing, and it isn't the same as the occasional forgetfulness everyone experiences. It's a progressive disease, which is precisely why catching it early changes what families can do about it. This 21 September, World Alzheimer's Day 2026 falls on a Sunday, within World Alzheimer's Month, a global observance running since 1994 and backed annually by the WHO. Over 55 million people worldwide live with dementia. In India, that's over 8.8 million people, roughly 7.4% of everyone above 60, a number expected to more than double by 2050. Only about 1 in 10 Indians with dementia ever gets diagnosed. If you're managing your parents' lives from another city, mostly through a WhatsApp group and a weekend visit, this day is really about one useful question: what can you do this week to help a parent's brain stay sharp for longer? Turns out, quite a lot Dr Harjit Singh, a geriatrician at Delhi's Sitaram Bhartia Institute, treats memory decline as something you can delay, not something inevitable. "Healthy ageing requires intention, support and opportunity," he says. Staying active, social and curious can help older adults maintain brain health. Photograph: (Nightingales Elder Care) His advice: “Eat together when you can, push for real exercise including strength training, nudge parents toward learning something new, and help them build an actual social circle rather than assuming living with family is company enough. His most millennial-coded tip: teach digital literacy through your own kids, since navigating an app gives an ageing brain a workout passive TV never will. Professor Prasun Chatterjee, who leads geriatric medicine at Apollo Hospitals after heading it at AIIMS Delhi, pushes this further in his book Health and Well-Being in Late Life, arguing old age deserves purpose, not just care. He built India's first Intergenerational Learning Model, where elderly volunteers teach underprivileged schoolchildren, giving retirees a real reason to think and show up daily. It's why structured volunteering or a community of older travellers does more for the brain than isolation. WHO guidelines agree, pointing to managing hypertension and diabetes, staying active, quitting smoking, eating well, and staying social as the most reliable ways to lower risk. It's bigger than sugar and blood pressure Dr Pranav Mehta, a neurologist at Apex Group of Hospitals, Mumbai, notes neurological disorders now affect over 30 million Indians and aren't just an "old people problem," with pollution and poor sleep playing a role too. His warning is the one to remember: "The brain often whispers before it screams," he says, listing slurred speech, sudden imbalance, vision changes or an unusual headache as signs never to brush off. Families can support ageing parents by encouraging independence, movement and meaningful daily routines. Photograph: (Scroll.in) Researchers also point to low formal education as a risk factor, meaning puzzles, reading and learning aren't a nice-to-have; they're real protection. The balance nobody warns you about None of this needs a medical degree. It needs attention, the kind that clocks when mom stops calling old friends, or a hobby quietly disappears. Geriatricians also warn against overprotection, which strips parents of the independence that keeps them active in the first place. Keep encouraging them to learn, move and connect, and stay alert enough to know when it's time for a doctor's opinion, not just another joke in the group chat. This World Alzheimer's Day, the best thing you can give your parents isn't a check-up booked and forgotten. It's making sure their days still have reasons to think, remember, and stay curious. title: Timaru woman finds rare moa bones during daily beach walk
content:
Timaru woman finds rare moa bones during daily beach walk
Family stumbles upon Moa bones on daily beach walk
A family is buzzing after a woman stumbled upon moa bones during her daily beach walk south of Timaru.
Pippa Yates found what she suspected to be the bones of the now-extinct New Zealand bird at St Andrews Beach, which the South Canterbury Museum confirmed after closer inspection.
Yates told Checkpoint the discovery was all the family could talk about.
"Anytime we get a spare moment, we clean the bones that we've got. We've got probably a good half a bucket full of moa bones now, so they're seemingly coming up a lot better than we expected they would," she said.
"The museum said they'd crumble apart, so far we've got some really big pieces that have actually made it through being cleaned very carefully."
Yates said the family were just using plain water to clean the bones to try and emulate natural washing on the beach.
She said she's had to sacrifice her daughter's plastic basin previously used for cleaning baby bottles.
"We put a bit of cold water over the bones, which are sort of still within clay in big chunks, and swish the water over them from side to side, let them sit for an hour or more, and then drain the water out and start again, being careful not to lose any of the tiny bits of bone as well, so it's a slow process," Yates said.
Yates said the family had been scaling the beach for about four years after hearing about a man finding a moa footprint and bones.
"I walk looking at my feet basically the entire time where we walk, specifically in all the clay banks, we always look in those areas thinking we might see a footprint, and that's something I can bring my daughter back to see," she said.
"We as a family have quite a collection of bones and oddities in our little bone cabinet at home, so we're quite familiar with the look of bone.
"The porosity of the bone, I could tell looking down on it that it looks sort of like a cross section of a bone as opposed to a piece of driftwood or something else stuck in the mud."
Yates' four-year-old daughter, Lucy, is part of an explorer club at the museum.
She said she's been going ever since she could walk.
"She's obsessed with the museum, and she knows where everything is and likes to show anybody that comes to visit us where everything is in the museum," Yates said.
"So yes, she's got a keen interest on all those kinds of things. Her dad has got her quite interested in it as well, if we find skeletal remains of any kind, dead bird, on the beach, we bag it up and bring it home for dad to make it into a display for our bone cabinet.
"We have quite a lot of seagulls and all sorts of things in the bone cabinet."
Yates said the family planned on keeping a few of the larger bones to possibly piece them together.
She hoped to put it on display in their home for visitors.
"But any of the really obviously bone-looking bones, we're going to try and give back the museum, which will be nice to have on display," she said.
"Molly's my daughter who was on my front while we were walking on the beach. So, when she has children one day, she can go and say, 'this is the bones that mum and I found when I was just a baby on her front' and her children and her great grandchildren and those kinds of things.
"It's a legacy to have it on display, and any of the tiny little bits of we're going to put in specimen jars and bring them to the (kindergarten) and the school to have a look at as well."

title: Jagtar Singh Johal granted bail nine years after being detained in India
content:
Jagtar Singh Johal granted bail nine years after being detained in India
- Published
A Scottish Sikh activist who has been locked up in India for almost nine years without conviction has been granted bail.
Jagtar Singh Johal, from Dumbarton, was arrested and detained in 2017 in connection with alleged terror offences.
The Indian authorities have accused him of having a role in a series of targeted killings of religious and political figures.
His family said they were still waiting for the details of what will happen next but are "relieved" by the Indian court's decision.
Court documents show Johal was granted bail at Delhi High Court.
As part of his bail conditions, he has to surrender his passport and is barred from speaking to the media about the case.
He must pay a personal bond of 500,000 rupees (£3,907) and is only allowed to access one phone.
The 39-year-old was acquitted last year in a case in which he was accused of financially supporting terror group the Khalistan Liberation Force (KLF), which has carried out attacks in the Punjab region.
But he still faces federal charges lodged by the Indian authorities.
Johal's imprisonment was recognised by a UN panel as arbitrary detention in 2022 and he has claimed to have been tortured.
Indian authorities have previously denied the torture claim and have repeatedly maintained due process is being followed.
He was arrested in the Punjab region just weeks after his wedding in the country.
His supporters say he was targeted for blogging about alleged human rights abuses against the Sikh community in India and was coerced into signing a false confession to participation in the killings.
His brother Gurpreet Singh Johal has lobbied successive governments calling for his brother's release.
"It is a really important milestone for Jagtar's campaign," Gurpreet told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme.
"It has been a long haul and an expensive rollercoaster but the community and the public have kept me going to campaign to bring Jagtar home.
"This will be a huge relief for him."
He added that while it is a major step and the family are relieved Jagtar can be at liberty, more work will be required to bring his brother back to Dumbarton.
"It is a momentous moment for the family, his wife has been crying since this morning," Gurpreet added.
"Everyone was joyful, my kids went to school saying they cannot wait to see their uncle coming home.
"It is just a first step, but it is a step in the right direction."
Gupreet previously urged the UK government to provide "diplomatic representation" to bring his activist brother home.
He described his last meeting, with then-Foreign secretary Yvette Cooper in December, as "disappointing".
At the time, a spokesperson for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office said concerns about Johal's "prolonged detention" were raised with the Indian government at every appropriate opportunity.
Johal was previously denied bail in 2024.
Johal's family have insisted that no concrete evidence has been presented against him.
They say the case was built on the testimony of unreliable witnesses, some of whom have given statements against him only for them to be later recanted in court.
'Flawed proceedings'
First Minister John Swinney said it was a "significant and positive development".
"I hope to see Mr Johal released from custody as soon as the necessary procedures are completed and continue to underline the importance of a fair, transparent and timely judicial process," he added.
Johal is represented in the UK by the legal charities Redress and Reprieve, which have welcomed the judgement.
Reprieve's deputy executive director Dan Dolan said the news was welcome but Johal still faces the death penalty for "trumped up charges".
He said: "We must now watch closely to ensure this order is actually implemented and not obstructed in any way.
"The conditions attached are likely to be onerous."
Redress senior legal advisor Chris Esdaile said granting bail "can't undo the intolerable suffering caused by nine years of arbitrary detention".
He added: "The need for accountability for the allegations of torture and the deeply flawed proceedings against Jagtar remains urgent."

title: Application of the electronic scoliometer in school-based scoliosis screening among elementary school students and analysis of factors associated with suspected scoliosis
content: BackgroundScoliosis imposes a growing health burden on school-age children in China, yet data specific to elementary school students aged 6–12 years remain scarce. This study aimed to compare the positive screening rate and screening efficiency of the electronic scoliometer (E-scoliometer) with those of the manual scoliometer (M-scoliometer), and to identify modifiable risk factors for suspected scoliosis in this younger age group.MethodsA school-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 11,587 students in grades 1–5 from 10 public elementary schools in Harbin, China (September 2024–May 2025), using multistage stratified cluster sampling. Classes were randomly allocated to the M-scoliometer group (n = 5,697 pupils) or the E-scoliometer group (n = 5,890). A stratified subsample of 3,600 students underwent posture assessment and parent-reported questionnaire survey. Associations were examined within two domains by binary logistic regression and then in a single joint generalized estimating equation (GEE) model providing mutual adjustment across domains and accounting for clustering of pupils within classes.ResultsThe overall positive screening rate was 1.61%, increasing significantly from Grade 1 (0.26%) to Grade 5 (2.89%; p < 0.001). The two devices yielded comparable positive screening rates (M-scoliometer 1.67% vs. E-scoliometer 1.56%; difference 0.11 percentage points, 95% CI − 0.36 to 0.57; p = 0.706), while the E-scoliometer reduced mean screening time by 54.2% (16.04 s vs. 35.00 s; p < 0.001). In the joint GEE model (59 events, 9 parameters, 6.56 events per variable, optimism-corrected AUC 0.910), flat back (OR = 7.36), picky eating (OR = 4.19), daily physical exercise < 1 h/day (OR = 3.86), mild wasting (OR = 3.80), shoulder height asymmetry (OR = 3.06) and higher grade (OR = 1.43 per grade) were associated with higher odds of suspected scoliosis, whereas regular adjustment of chair and desk height (OR = 0.18) and regular rotation of classroom seating (OR = 0.19) were associated with lower odds. The association with thumb-inward grip pen-holding posture did not persist under mutual adjustment (OR = 1.55, 95% CI 0.77–3.11) and is reported as hypothesis-generating.ConclusionThe E-scoliometer yielded a positive screening rate comparable to that of the M-scoliometer with markedly superior efficiency, supporting its adoption in large-scale school-based programs. The factors identified were largely modifiable, suggesting that promoting daily physical activity, improving nutritional behaviors, and standardizing classroom furniture management and seating rotation merit consideration in school-based scoliosis prevention strategies for elementary school children.

title: NT Aboriginal leaders' resignations come with an explosive exit note
content:
analysis
String of NT Aboriginal leaders resign, claiming CLP government policies are 'dividing' Territorians
After resigning from her position as the boss of Aboriginal Housing Northern Territory this week, Leeanne Caton came out swinging.
Her target: the NT's Country Liberal Party (CLP) government, which was elected in a landslide in 2024 on a mandate to tackle crime and anti-social behaviour.
Since the CLP's election, it has overhauled laws on bail, youth criminal responsibility and child protection, and given police a range of new powers.
NT Police say the territory has been recording lower crime rates following the changes.
But Ms Caton said she believed this was all done without listening to Aboriginal leadership.
"The reason why I'm leaving is basically every piece of legislation that gets put through has a negative impact directly on Aboriginal people," the Kalkadoon-Waanyi woman told ABC Radio Darwin.
"It's killing my spirit.
"I just can't stand to see what's happening to Aboriginal Territorians in this environment at the moment."
The straw that broke the camel's back for Ms Caton was the handling of the future of a Darwin homeless shelter, which is being shifted to the regional town of Batchelor.
The departure of the peak body boss is the latest in a string of resignations by Aboriginal leaders and organisations in the Territory over fraying relationships with the NT government.
Among them, the NT Children's Commissioner Shahleena Musk, independent chair of the NT Children and Families Tripartite Forum Rob McPhee, Darwin Waterfront Corporation chairman Richard Fejo, members of the NT Justice Policy Partnership and independent Arnhem Land parliamentarian, Yiŋiya Guyula.
All have made public statements about their decisions to quit and, while each has been for a different reason, they have all shared ideological opposition to the NT government's laws or policies, with most citing an inability to have their voices heard.
'Still considered flora and fauna'
Now back in the Arnhem Land bush, Mr Guyula was asked for his reaction to Ms Caton's resignation and the current relationship between Aboriginal leaders and the CLP.
"They are creating a significant divide that is harming the NT," he said.
"They are tearing us all apart by treating our people as though we are not human, as though we are … considered flora and fauna."
He described the CLP's move to relocate the homeless shelter as "about dividing people in an attempt to push our people out of Darwin".
"It just does more harm to everyone," he said.
Former NT Labor politician and long-term First Nations advocate Scott McConnell said he feared diminishing trust between Aboriginal groups and the government was damaging the jurisdiction's future prospects.
"The geography of the NT is vast [but] the community is very small," he said.
"Governments need to stop dividing us based on race and geography and remember we have one shared future.
"I am very concerned that prominent leaders I know, trust and respect are finding the current environment so difficult they are leaving the front line.
"We all need to continue to support these fighters."
CLP government denies division
The NT's Acting Chief Minister Gerard Maley has fiercely defended the government's relationship with Aboriginal people and communities following the resignations.
Mr Maley also said his government stood by its continued focus on stamping out crime.
"We are listening to Aboriginal people," he said in a press conference on Friday.
"We work with many, many Aboriginal organisations right across the NT.
"And we need to work with them because we need to make sure the Aboriginal sector continues because there are a lot of Aboriginal people here.
"We want to make sure [their] safety is also our number one priority, and we're going to work with anyone we can to make sure that happens."
Mr Maley took issue with a question about why Aboriginal people were shut out of the conversation around the homeless shelter's move to Batchelor.
"We've been working with all sorts of organisations about that," he said.
In her parting shots at the NT government, Ms Caton vehemently disagreed: “It’s [been] disrespect and a lack of courtesy all round.”
Despite the vocal criticism and walk-outs, the government continues its mission towards a safer territory; no matter who argues against the way it’s going about it.

title: Charlotte Englebert et Félix Radu promus "Étincelles de Wallonie"
